subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 20-year-old woman with phenylketonuria maintains a low-phenylalanine diet and has stable plasma phenylalanine levels. At a party she drinks several sugar-free beverages sweetened with aspartame, and her plasma phenylalanine rises the next day.
question: Which of the following best explains this increase?

options.text: Aspartame is hydrolyzed to tyrosine and homogentisic acid.
Aspartame is hydrolyzed in the gut to phenylalanine and aspartate.
Aspartame is converted by gut bacteria to phenylketones.

explanation_correct: Aspartame is a methyl ester of the dipeptide aspartate-phenylalanine, so it releases phenylalanine when hydrolyzed in the intestine. Patients with phenylketonuria must avoid aspartame because they cannot convert the additional phenylalanine to tyrosine, and their plasma phenylalanine can rise substantially.

explanation_incorrect.A: Phenylalanine hydroxylase is already deficient in phenylketonuria; aspartame does not inhibit the enzyme further.
explanation_incorrect.B: Aspartame does not contain homogentisic acid and is not hydrolyzed to it.
explanation_incorrect.C: Aspartame is a source of amino acids, not a tetrahydrobiopterin antagonist.
explanation_incorrect.E: Phenylketones are produced endogenously from accumulated phenylalanine, not by bacterial metabolism of aspartame.

educationalObjective: Aspartame releases phenylalanine and must be avoided by patients with phenylketonuria.
